subject: Multilevel Regression too computationally expensive, probably implemented incorrectly

messages.author: 83b63066408210ec
messages.subject: Multilevel Regression too computationally expensive, probably implemented incorrectly
parts:
I first asked this question on Cross Validated, where it probably has better visualisation.

I have, for N_countries countries and for each day during a certain period, a list of purchases from my website and how much each purchase was. I think that money spent as a function of days since the start of this period follows a sigmoid.

I want to model this according to a multilevel model, in which some of the parametres are drawn from distributions whose hyperparametres are drawn from another distribution (my population level is the country). The way I did it is, however, incredibly computationally expensive:

   
data {
      int<lower = 1> N_people_day;
      int<lower = 1> N_countries;
      int<lower = 1, upper = N_countries> country[N_people_day];
      int<lower = 0> dsi[N_people_day];
      vector<lower = 0>[N_people_day] net_revenue;
    }
   
    parameters {
      // parametres
      vector<lower = 0>[N_countries] scale;                       // the sigmoid's scale parametre
      real<lower = 0> rate;                                       // rate parametre
      real<lower = 0> x_location;                                 // location parametre
      vector<lower = 0>[N_countries] y_location;                  // location parametre
      real<lower = 0> sigma;                                      // dispersion parametre
     
      // hyperparametres
      real<lower = 0> y_location_hyper_shape;
      real<lower = 0> y_location_hyper_rate;
      real<lower = 0> scale_hyper_shape;
      real<lower = 0> scale_hyper_rate;
    }
   
    transformed parameters {
      vector[N_people_day] mu;
     
      for(i in 1:N_people_day){
        mu[i] = scale[country[i]] / (1 + exp(-(rate * dsi[i] + x_location))) + y_location[country[i]];
      }
    }
   
    model {
      net_revenue ~ normal(mu, sigma);
      y_location ~ gamma(y_location_hyper_shape, y_location_hyper_rate);
      x_location ~ gamma(10, 0.5);
      scale ~ gamma(scale_hyper_shape, scale_hyper_rate);
    }


I'm almost certain there's a better way to do it and that the biggest problem is that one for in the transformed parameters block. How should I do it instead, though?

messages.author: da33143a8db60ce8
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Multilevel Regression too computationally expensive, probably implemented incorrectly
parts:
Hi, just a couple quick comments.  There's something kinda weird about your model because the data are positive but you're fitting a normal model with additive errors.  Can't net_revenue be negative sometimes?  Why must it be positive.  Also in your expression for mu, you can simplify the code by vectorzing (just omit the subscripts [i] and take it out of a loop), also use the inv_logit function if that's what you want.  But I don't think this inv_logit thing makes much sense either.  Also it doesn't look right that y_location is additive with a gamma distribution.  Lots of things about this model look odd.  I recommend you re-think it from first principles, as what you have below looks like a mash-up of distributions with no underlying model.
A

parts:
Hello!

net_revenue cannot be negative - a purchase can only give me money, it cannot take money from me - and the model assumption is "a purchase on a given day will give me a value of money that follows a logistic function of the day plus random noise."

Trying to omit the subscripts [i] gives me an error: it says there are no matches for real * int[]. If I convert all my int[] to vectors I get no matches for vector / vector, plus "Container index must be integer" at scale[country].

The inv_logit thing is mostly because, empirically, it looks like my data behaves like that: the average is mostly constant for a while, then it grows, then it becomes mostly constant at a new value afterwards.

The model doesn't really have a lot going for it in the way of first principles - what I want to do is just a regression, because it seemed like what made the most sense but I'm not super confident in this.

Pedro

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Multilevel Regression too computationally expensive, probably implemented incorrectly
parts:
No, Stan provides no real to integer conversion on purpose.
Its algorithms are aimed at continuously differentiable densities.

> On Dec 16, 2016, at 5:31 PM, Pedro Carvalho <pedro...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> In this case the "net" is gross times 0.7. How would I model the multiplicative, exactly?

lognormal.

That's an unusual net function. Usually it's income minus costs
and the costs aren't constant proportions of the gross.

> And my biggest problem is exactly with the vectorisation part: that for takes forever to run, but even the example linear regression model on git uses a for rather than vectorisation so I don't know if it's possible at all.

Yes, you can vectorize. We just added a bunch of language features
like general vectorization in 2.13 so we'll sweep through and update
all the models soon, but we probably won't be done until well into next
year.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Multilevel Regression too computationally expensive, probably implemented incorrectly
parts:
We follow math conventions. Real * vector is just that: a * b. If you need vector multiplied by vector, that must be elementwise multiplication.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Multilevel Regression too computationally expensive, probably implemented incorrectly
parts:
> On Dec 17, 2016, at 9:21 AM, Pedro Carvalho <pedro...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Right, but when I try doing real * vector it gives me the vector / vector error

If you have (real * vector), the result is vector. Same with (vector * real).
You can do (row_vector * vector) and get a real, or (vector * row_vector)
and get a matrix. But you can't do (vector * vector) because the dimensions
don't conform to matrix multiplication.
> (which cannot really be corrected by pointwise division because the vectors' sizes are different),

Do you have a simple example of the types you want
to define and operations you want to perform? We can help
with specifics of error messages.
> and there's also the problem where scale[country] doesn't work because country is a vector (even though what I really mean is scale[country[i]] for every i, as defined in the for loop).

country is going to be an array if it's an index. and if
it's an array of K elements, then scale[country] will also
have K elements, (scale[country[1]], ..., scale[country[K]])

- Bob
